On stability of self-similar blowup for mass supercritical NLS

Zexing Li Address: Laboratoire AGM
CY Cergy Paris Université
2 avenue Adolphe Chauvin
95300 Pontoise
France Email address: zexing.li@u-cergy.fr
Abstract.

We consider the mass supercritical (NLS) i​∂tu+Δ​u+u​|u|p−1=0i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}=0 in dimension d≥1d\geq 1 in the mass-supercritical range 0<sc=d2−2p−1<10<s_{c}=\frac{d}{2}-\frac{2}{p-1}<1. The existence of self-similar blow up dyamics is known [51], and suitable self-similar blow up profiles were constructed in [2]. In this work, we establish the finite codimensional nonlinear asymptotic stability in homogeneous Sobolev space and energy space H1H^{1} for a large class of self-similar profiles. The heart of the proof is, following the approach of Beceanu [4], the derivation of Strichartz dispersive estimates for matrix operators of the form

ℋ=(Δb−1−Δ−b+1)−i​b​sc+(W1W2−W2¯−W1),\mathcal{H}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\Delta_{b}-1&\\ &-\Delta_{-b}+1\end{array}\right)-ibs_{c}+\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}W_{1}&W_{2}\\ -\overline{W_{2}}&-W_{1}\end{array}\right),

b>0b>0 and

Δb=Δ+ib(d2+x⋅∇),\Delta_{b}=\Delta+ib\left(\frac{d}{2}+x\cdot\nabla\right),

inhomogeneous Sobolev spaces. The deformed Laplacian Δb\Delta_{b} arises from the renormalization and its operator group ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} exhibits self-similar dispersion, which not only recovers the free Strichartz but also enables an extension of resolvent families. Compared with Strichartz estimates based on Δ\Delta, this one has a larger admissible region, works for arbitrarily small polynomial decaying potential, and requires no spectral assumption.

1. Introduction

1.1. Setting of the problem

We consider the nonlinear Schrödinger equation

{i​∂tu+Δ​u+u​|u|p−1=0u|t=0=u0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}=0\\ u_{|t=0}=u_{0}\end{array}\right. (NLS)

for spatial dimension d≥1d\geq 1 and p>1p>1. The scaling symmetry

uλ​(t,x):=λ2p−1​u​(λ2​t,λ​x),λ>0u_{\lambda}(t,x):=\lambda^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x),\quad\lambda>0

allows us to compute the critical Sobolev norm invariant

‖uλ​(t,⋅)‖H˙sc=‖u⁡(λ2​t,⋅)‖H˙sc,sc:=d2−2p−1.\|u_{\lambda}(t,\cdot)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}}=\|u(\lambda^{2}t,\cdot)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}},\quad s_{c}:=\frac{d}{2}-\frac{2}{p-1}.

In this paper, we are interested in describing singularity formation mechanisms for nonlinearities above the mass and below the energy conservation laws:

0<sc<1.0<s_{c}<1.

1.2. Type I and Type II blowup.

We now recall some key facts related to the description of singularity formation for (NLS) with 0<sc<10<s_{c}<1.

The self-similar law. From an elementary scaling argument, all blow up solutions satisfy the scaling self-similar lower bound

‖u⁡(t)‖H˙σ≳(T−t)−σ−sc2\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\gtrsim(T-t)^{-\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}} (1.1)

where sc<σ≤1s_{c}<\sigma\leq 1 is supercritical. We say a solution blows up self-similarily if it saturates the self-similar law

‖u⁡(t)‖H˙σ∼(T−t)−σ−sc2,sc<σ≤1.\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\sim(T-t)^{-\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}},\quad s_{c}<\sigma\leq 1. (1.2)

Type II blow. Type II solutions which blow up strictly faster than (1.2) have been constructed both in the critical case sc=0s_{c}=0, [53, 44, 46, 42, 43, 45, 54]), and the supercritical case through the derivation of "ring" solutions which concentrate on a circle, [22, 55, 52, 29].

Type I blow. However, for 0<sc<10<s_{c}<1, type I blow is conjectured to exist and generate stable blow up dynamics, [63, 62]. More precisely, the self-similar renormalization

u⁡(t,x)=ei​γ​(t)(λ⁡(t))2p−1​v​(τ,y)u(t,x)=\frac{e^{i\gamma(t)}}{(\lambda(t))^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}v\left(\tau,y\right)

with the explicit laws

λ⁡(t)=2​b​(T−t),γ⁡(t)=τ⁡(t),τ⁡(t)=−12​b​ln⁡(T−t),y=xλ⁡(t)\lambda(t)=\sqrt{2b(T-t)},\quad\gamma(t)=\tau(t),\ \ \tau(t)=-\frac{1}{2b}\ln(T-t),\ \ y=\frac{x}{\lambda(t)} (1.3)

maps (NLS) onto the renormalized flow

i​∂τv+Δ​v−v+i​b2​(2p−1​v+y⋅∇v)+v​|v|p−1=0.i\partial_{\tau}v+\Delta v-v+\frac{ib}{2}\left(\frac{2}{p-1}v+y\cdot\nabla v\right)+v|v|^{p-1}=0. (1.4)

In the range 0<sc<10<s_{c}<1, admissible self-similar profiles are expected to exist from numerical grounds, [41, 36, 35, 62, 6, 5].

Conjecture (Existence of suitable profiles). Let d≥1d\geq 1 and sc∈(0,1)s_{c}\in(0,1). Then there exists b=b⁡(d,sc)>0b=b(d,s_{c})>0 and a smooth radially symmetric profile QbQ_{b} with the following properties.11 1 The equation (1.5) and self-similar decay (1.7) are essential, in that they can imply the non-vanishing property (1.6) and self-similar decay for higher order derivatives (1.8) via ODE analysis, see [66, Lemma 2.2] and [37] respectively. We remark that the main result of [66] was unfortunately dubious.

  1. (i)

    Equation: QbQ_{b} is a stationary solution to (1.4):

    Δ​Qb−Qb+i​b​(2p−1​Qb+y⋅∇Qb)+Qb​|Qb|p−1=0.\Delta Q_{b}-Q_{b}+ib\left(\frac{2}{p-1}Q_{b}+y\cdot\nabla Q_{b}\right)+Q_{b}|Q_{b}|^{p-1}=0. (1.5)
  2. (ii)

    Non-vanishing:

    Qb​(x)≠0∀x∈ℝd.Q_{b}(x)\neq 0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (1.6)
  3. (iii)

    Self-similar decay:

    limr→∞r2p−1​|Qb​(r)|=cp>0,\displaystyle\mathop{\rm lim}_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{2}{p-1}}|Q_{b}(r)|=c_{p}>0, lim supr→∞rp+1p−1​|Qb′​(r)|<∞;\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}|Q_{b}^{\prime}(r)|<\infty; (1.7)
    lim supr→∞r2p−1+k​|∂rkQb′​(r)|<∞,\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{2}{p-1}+k}|\partial_{r}^{k}Q_{b}^{\prime}(r)|<\infty, ∀k≥2.\displaystyle\forall\,\,k\geq 2. (1.8)

The existence of such profiles has been obtained by Bahri-Martel-Raphaël [2] in the range 0<sc≪10<s_{c}\ll 1 by bifurcating from the critical case sc=0s_{c}=0, see also [33] for the case of (gKdV). Extending the branch to higher values of scs_{c} is a delicate nonlinear ODE problem, and recently Donninger-Shörkhuber [17] constructed the suitable profile for the physical scenario d=p=3d=p=3 with computer assistance. Let us stress that the construction of self-similar profiles is central in the study of singularity formation mechanisms and has been mostly addressed in the energy supercritical case sc>1s_{c}>1, see [12] for the heat equation, [13] for the wave equation and [28, 50] for compressible fluids.

Existence of self-similar dynamics. Self-similar profiles satisfying (1.7) are not in the energy space H1H^{1} and hence cannot be used as such to produce finite energy type I solutions. The existence of such dynamics was first obtained in [51] for 0<sc≪10<s_{c}\ll 1 using again a bifurcation argument from the critical case sc=0s_{c}=0. The analysis provides solutions that satisfy the self-similar law (1.1), but does not describe the asymptotic structure of the singularity which should be given by the self-similar profile constructed in [2].

1.3. Main results

Our aim in this paper is to provide a robust approach for the proof of the asymptotic stability of self-similar profiles.

1.3.1. H˙sc+\dot{H}^{s_{c}+} stability theory

Theorem 1.1 (Finite-codimensional asymptotic stability in H˙sc+\dot{H}^{s_{c}+}).

Let d≥1d\geq 1, sc∈(0,1)s_{c}\in(0,1), and b,Qbb,Q_{b} satisfying (1.5), (1.6), (1.7). Then for any 0<σ−sc≪10<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1, there exists a Lipschitz finite-codimensional manifold ℳ⊂H˙σ\mathcal{M}\subset\dot{H}^{\sigma} of initial data

u0=Qb+ε0u_{0}=Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0}

where ‖ε0‖H˙σ≪1\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\ll 1, such that the corresponding solution to (NLS) blows up at T=12​bT=\frac{1}{2b} with a decomposition

u⁡(t,x)=1λ​(t)2p−1​(Qb+ε)​(t,xλ⁡(t))​ei​τ​(t)u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda(t)^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}(Q_{b}+\varepsilon)\left(t,\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}\right)e^{i\tau(t)} (1.9)

where (λ⁡(t),γ⁡(t),τ⁡(t))(\lambda(t),\gamma(t),\tau(t)) are given by (1.3) and

‖ε⁡(t)‖H˙xσ≲(T−t)σ−sc2.\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{x}}\lesssim(T-t)^{\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}}. (1.10)

Moreover, there exists u∗∈H˙σu_{*}\in\dot{H}^{\sigma} such that

u⁡(t)−1λ​(t)2p−1​Qb​(xλ⁡(t))​ei​τ​(t)→u∗in​H˙σa​st→T.u(t)-\frac{1}{\lambda(t)^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}Q_{b}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}\right)e^{i\tau(t)}\to u_{*}\quad\mathrm{in}\,\,\dot{H}^{\sigma}\quad as\quad t\to T. (1.11)

The result reduces the nonlinear asymptotic stability to a linear spectral stability problem. As a corollary, assuming the unstable directions of the linearized operator are generated merely by symmetries of the equation (mode stability), we can obtain the asymptotic stability without losing codimensions.

Assumption 1.2 (Mode stability).

Let d≥1,sc∈(0,1)d\geq 1,s_{c}\in(0,1), and b,Qbb,Q_{b} satisfying (1.5), (1.6), (1.7). Let ℋ{\mathcal{H}} be the linearized operator around QbQ_{b} in self-similar coordinates defined by (1.4)-(1.26). For any 0<σ−sc≪10<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1, the discrete spectrum of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} satisfies

σdisc​(ℋ|(H˙σ​(ℝd))2)∩{z∈ℂ:ℑ⁡z<b⁡(σ−sc)}={0,−b​i,−2​b​i},\sigma_{\rm disc}\left({\mathcal{H}}\big|_{(\dot{H}^{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}}\right)\cap\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z<b(\sigma-s_{c})\right\}=\{0,-bi,-2bi\}, (1.12)

with the corresponding Riesz projections satisfying22 2 They are instabilities generated by phase rotation, spatial translation and scaling symmetry respectively. See Section 6.3 for detailed discussion.

dimRan​P0=1,dimRan​P−b​i=d,dimRan​P−2​b​i=1.\dim{\rm Ran}P_{0}=1,\quad\dim{\rm Ran}P_{-bi}=d,\quad\dim{\rm Ran}P_{-2bi}=1. (1.13)
Remark 1.3 (Verification of mode stability).

Proving Assumption 1.2 for certain self-similar profile is an independent linear problem. It requires an exact characterization of unstable spectrum for a non-self-adjoint operator, which is relatively unbounded with respect to (matrix) Schrödinger operators. In our forthcoming work [37], we show this property holds for the slightly mass-supercritical profiles constructed in [2] for d≤10d\leq 10, as expected from the stability result [51].

Theorem 1.4 (Conditional asymptotical stability in H˙sc+\dot{H}^{s_{c}+}).

Under the same assumption of Theorem 1.1 plus mode stability Assumption 1.2, for any 0<σ−sc≪10<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1, there exists ϵ1≪1\epsilon_{1}\ll 1 such that for all ‖ε0‖H˙σ<ϵ1\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}<\epsilon_{1}, there uniquely exists (λ0,x0,θ0)∈ℝ×ℝd×ℝ(\lambda_{0},x_{0},\theta_{0})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with

|λ0−1|+|x0|+|θ0|≲‖ε0‖H˙σ\displaystyle|\lambda_{0}-1|+|x_{0}|+|\theta_{0}|\lesssim\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}

such that the initial data u0=Qb+ε0u_{0}=Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0} generates a solution blowing up at T=λ022​bT=\frac{\lambda_{0}^{2}}{2b} satisfying the decomposition

u⁡(t,x)=1(1−2​b​λ0−2​t)1p−1​(Qb+ε)​(t,x−x0λ02−2​b​t)​e−i⁡[ln⁡(12​b−λ0−2​t)2​b+θ0]u(t,x)=\frac{1}{(1-2b\lambda_{0}^{-2}t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}}(Q_{b}+\varepsilon)\left(t,\frac{x-x_{0}}{\sqrt{\lambda_{0}^{2}-2bt}}\right)e^{-i\left[\frac{\ln(\frac{1}{2b}-\lambda_{0}^{-2}t)}{2b}+\theta_{0}\right]} (1.14)

with the decaying of perturbation (1.10) and the existence of blowup profile in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} (1.11).

Comments on Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4.

1. Regularity. (NLS) is local-wellposed in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} with 0<σ−sc≪10<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1, see Proposition D.1, so the evolution makes sense with merely u0∈H˙σu_{0}\in\dot{H}^{\sigma}. This result is almost sharp in terms of regularity for H˙s\dot{H}^{s} spaces, and the critical H˙sc\dot{H}^{s_{c}} stability is still open.

2. Manifold structure of Theorem 1.1. Let Bϵ0H˙σ:={f∈H˙σ,‖f‖H˙σ<ϵ0}B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}:=\{f\in\dot{H}^{\sigma},\|f\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}<\epsilon_{0}\} with ϵ0≪1\epsilon_{0}\ll 1, then we construct a direct sum decomposition

H˙σ=Xu⊕Xc​s\dot{H}^{\sigma}=X_{u}\oplus X_{cs} (1.15)

with Xc​sX_{cs} and XuX_{u} are ℝ\mathbb{R}-linear subspaces and XuX_{u} finite-dimensional, and a Lipschitz map Φ:Bϵ0H˙σ∩Xc​s→Xu\Phi:B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs}\to X_{u} with Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(0)=0, such that the manifold in Theorem 1.1 can be realized as

ℳ=(Id+Φ)​(Bϵ0H˙σ∩Xc​s)+Qb.\mathcal{M}=({\rm Id}+\Phi)(B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs})+Q_{b}. (1.16)

Moreover, this manifold is tangential to the center-stable hyperplane Bϵ0H˙σ∩Xc​s+QbB_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs}+Q_{b}. See Theorem 6.4 for more accurate formulation.

1.4. Strichartz estimates for the self-similar propagator

Let the deformed Laplacian be

Δb:=Δ+ib(d2+y⋅∇).\displaystyle\Delta_{b}:=\Delta+ib\left(\frac{d}{2}+y\cdot\nabla\right).

Structure of the linearized operator. The linearization of the time-dependent flow (1.4) close to a self-similar solution QbQ_{b} solution to (1.5) leads to a non-self-adjoint linearized problem of the form

i​∂τZ+ℋ​Z=F⁡(Z).i\partial_{\tau}Z+{\mathcal{H}}Z=F(Z). (1.21)

Here FF is the nonlinear term, Z=(Z1Z2)∈ℂ2Z=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}Z_{1}\\ Z_{2}\end{array}\right)\in\mathbb{C}^{2} and

ℋ=(Δb−1−Δ−b+1)−i​b​sc+(W1W2−W¯2−W1)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\Delta_{b}-1&\\ &-\Delta_{-b}+1\end{array}\right)-ibs_{c}+\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}W_{1}&W_{2}\\ -\overline{W}_{2}&-W_{1}\end{array}\right)

for the explicit potentials

W1=p+12​|Qb|p−1,\displaystyle W_{1}=\frac{p+1}{2}|Q_{b}|^{p-1}, W2=p−12​Qb2​|Qb|p−3\displaystyle\quad W_{2}=\frac{p-1}{2}Q_{b}^{2}|Q_{b}|^{p-3} (1.26)

which under (1.7) satisfy a polynomial decay

|Wi​(x)|≲⟨x⟩−α,|∇Wi​(x)|≲⟨x⟩−α−1|W_{i}(x)|\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha},\quad|\nabla W_{i}(x)|\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha-1} (1.27)

for i=1,2i=1,2 for some α>0\alpha>0.

Decay for the linearized operator. Various strategies have been used in the literature to address the derivation of local-in-space decay estimates for linearized operators close to self-similar profiles: local Virial estimates [39, 44, 48], self-adjoint spectral estimates [12], distorted Fourier transform [34], semigroup estimates [16, 49, 32]. Strichartz estimates were derived in the pioneering work [14] to control the flow around self-similar blowup of spherically symmetric 3D energy-critical nonlinear wave equations in the renormalized light cone.

Strichartz bound. Our second main result in this paper is the derivation of global in space Strichartz estimates which can be directly used for the proof of the nonlinear stability Theorem 1.1. One edge of Strichartz estimate here, compared with semigroup method, is that it requires at most one derivative, hence works nicely for weak and non-analytic nonlinearities.

Our approach follows the framework developed by Beceanu for the derivation of Strichartz in the b=0b=0 case.

Theorem 1.6 (Strichartz estimates).

Let d≥1d\geq 1, b>0b>0 and sc∈(0,1)s_{c}\in(0,1). Let the linear matrix Schrödinger system,

i​∂τZ+ℋ​Z=Fi\partial_{\tau}Z+\mathcal{H}Z=F (1.28)

with ℋ\mathcal{H} as in (1.4), W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} satisfying (1.27) for some α>0\alpha>0. Then there exists δ1>0\delta_{1}>0 such that for all σ∈(sc,sc+δ1)\sigma\in(s_{c},s_{c}+\delta_{1}), there exists a finite rank projection operator Pdisc:H˙σ→H˙σP_{\rm disc}:\dot{H}^{\sigma}\to\dot{H}^{\sigma} such that the following holds. Let ν≤b⁡(σ−sc)\nu\leq b(\sigma-s_{c}) and Pess:=Id−PdiscP_{\rm ess}:={\rm Id}-P_{\rm disc}, then

where (qi,pi)(q_{i},p_{i}) for i=1,2i=1,2 satisfies

Comments on Theorem 1.6.

1. Deformed Laplacian Δb\Delta_{b}.

Compared with the standard Laplacian Δ\Delta, the correction part ib(d2+y⋅∇)ib(\frac{d}{2}+y\cdot\nabla) is not relatively bounded and changes the spectrum drastically to be σ⁡(Δb)=ℝ\sigma(\Delta_{b})=\mathbb{R} with b≠0b\neq 0 (see Lemma 2.5). Current results for variable-coefficient Schrödinger operators (for example [7, 61, 40]) do not directly apply since Δb\Delta_{b} is no longer asymptotically flat. Fortunately, the semigroup ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} enjoys good structure and has explicit representation (2.2)-(2.3) (first derived by Carles in [9, 10]). Here we list two main features:

  1. (1)

    H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma}-energy decay. The commutator of Δb\Delta_{b} with fractional differentiation DσD^{\sigma} gives constant i​b​σib\sigma, leading to an exponential decay eb​σ​te^{b\sigma t} of ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} as indicated in (1.29).

  2. (2)

    Self-similar dispersion. The self-similar rescaling in time makes ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} exhibit exponential dispersive decay as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. As an important corollary, the resolvent families can be extended onto and even beyond the real axis.

2. Comparison with Donninger’s work [14]. In [14], Donninger first represents the semigroup et​𝐋e^{t\mathbf{L}} by resolvents (λ−𝐋)−1(\lambda-\mathbf{L})^{-1} via Laplace transform, and further solves for Green’s functions to represent the resolvents. Then et​𝐋e^{t\mathbf{L}} is a sum of free part and perturbation given by potential, and Strichartz estimates of each part follow intricate spatial estimates. This explicit construction is very clear in treating the radial case.

In this work, we exploit nice structure of the free operator group ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} and deal with the potential with a more abstract framework invented by Beceanu [4], which utilizes the convolution structure of the semigroup and resolvent identities to reduce the Strichartz estimates to a uniform invertibility problem. The semigroup ei​t​ℋe^{it{\mathcal{H}}} is decomposed into a composition of the free part and the potentials (Birman-Schwinger principle) rather than a summation. This strategy avoids explicitly solving resolvent equations and thus can handle non-radial case in the whole space.

3. Comparison with Strichartz estimates for Schrödinger equation with potentials. There have been many works devoting to Strichartz estimates of ei​t​(−Δ+W)e^{it(-\Delta+W)} or its matrix version, arising from Schrödinger equation with potentials or linearization around solitons [14, 30, 59, 8, 25]. Since we replace the Laplace with a deformed one Δb\Delta_{b}, our Strichartz estimates have the following new features:

  1. (1)

    Enlarged admissible region of (q,p)(q,p). The self-similar dispersive rate at infinity implies a larger admissible region (1.30) (Figure 1) for ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}} (2.6) and ultimately for ei​t​ℋe^{it{\mathcal{H}}}, instead of just 2q+dp=d2\frac{2}{q}+\frac{d}{p}=\frac{d}{2}.

  2. (2)

    Decay of potential. To make the potential perturbative in ei​t​(−Δ+V)e^{it(-\Delta+V)}, we need at least |x|−2|x|^{-2} decay of VV (see [26] for counterexamples). However, the deformed case b≠0b\neq 0 can admit arbitrarily small polynomial decay (α>0\alpha>0 in the sense of (1.27)). This amounts to different boundedness of the limiting extension (−Δ−(λ+i​0))−1(-\Delta-(\lambda+i0))^{-1} and (−Δb−(λ+i​0))−1(-\Delta_{b}-(\lambda+i0))^{-1}.

  3. (3)

    No spectral assumption. Previous results usually assume the absence of resonance or embedded eigenvalues [59, 20], especially in the scenario of matrix-valued complex-valued potential [4, 25]. They would essentially affect the dispersive behavior, see [20] for more discussion. However, we can avoid that trouble by changing spaces H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} thanks to those two features of Δb\Delta_{b}. When σ\sigma varies, the H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma}-decay implies a shift of essential spectrum, while the discrete spectrum basically remains the same by uniform treatment with extended resolvent families. This decoupling effect allows us to avoid embedded exceptional values.

4. Finiteness of discrete spectrum. The operator PdiscP_{\rm disc} is the Riesz projection for discrete spectrum of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} (see Proposition 4.5). While the discrete spectra may accumulate toward the essential spectrum (see [4, Proposition 2.9]) for Schrödinger operator, the finite rank of PdiscP_{\rm disc} is an implication of the self-similar dispersion. This unconditional finiteness of unstable spectrum for linearized operator around blowup can also be proven through semigroup theory (see [49] or [24]).

5. Restriction on σ\sigma. The condition 0<σ−sc≪10<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1 is only to ensure the absence of exceptional value on essential spectrum by the decoupling effect. We also obtain H˙σ∩H˙1\dot{H}^{\sigma}\cap\dot{H}^{1} Strichartz (Lemma 7.2) as persistence of regularity for linear equation, and generalization to higher regularity is well-expected. However, due to the existence of embedded resonance ℋ​(i​Qb,−i​Qb¯)T=0{\mathcal{H}}(iQ_{b},-i\overline{Q_{b}})^{T}=0, the Strichartz estimate at sharp regularity is very unclear, even for the radial case44 4 For wave equation, the linearized operator has no embedding eigenmode in radial case, but has one generated by Lorentz symmetry in the non-radial case.

1.5. Outline of the proofs and the paper.

1.5.1. Proof of Strichartz estimates.

We proof Theorem 1.6 in Section 2-5 following the framework of Beceanu [4].

Step 1. Spectral analysis for scalar operators.

In Section 2, we will prove self-similar dispersive estimate and free Strichartz estimate for Δb\Delta_{b} as a self-adjoint operator on L2L^{2}, extend resolvent families as bounded operators from Lp′L^{p^{\prime}} to LpL^{p} (p>2)(p>2) and discuss their properties as resolvents. Since ℒ⁡(Lp′→Lp){\mathcal{L}}(L^{p^{\prime}}\to L^{p}) is no longer an algebra, we make sense of the resolvent identities and differentiability in a weighted L2L^{2} space to exploit oscillation in the Fourier space.

Next, in Section 3, we consider scalar operator V¯2​(−Δb−z)−1​V¯1{\overline{V}}_{2}(-\Delta_{b}-z)^{-1}{\overline{V}}_{1} in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} with scalar potentials V¯1,V¯2{\overline{V}}_{1},{\overline{V}}_{2} and prove its compactness and decay in zz.

Step 2. Spectral analysis for matrix operators. We come back to the matrix operator ℋ{\mathcal{H}} in Section 4. By decomposing V=V1​V2V=V_{1}V_{2}, the previous results ensure I+V2​(ℋ−V−z)−1​V1I+V_{2}({\mathcal{H}}-V-z)^{-1}V_{1} analytic Fredholm as bounded operators in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} with zz in a region independent of σ\sigma. Hence by picking σ\sigma close to scs_{c}, we can identify and decouple the discrete spectrum with the essential spectrum, and discuss their spectral Riesz projections PdiscP_{\rm disc} and PessP_{\rm ess}.

We conclude by confirming PessP_{\rm ess} eliminates all singularities of (ℋ−z)−1({\mathcal{H}}-z)^{-1}.

Step 3. Abstract Wiener’s theorem and end of the proof. In [4], Beceanu proved the abstract Wiener’s theorem which determines the invertibility of an operator in a convolutional Banach algebra through the invertibility of its Fourier transform. Since the Strichartz estimate for ei​τ​ℋe^{i\tau{\mathcal{H}}} can be reduced to invertibility of I−i​V2​ei​τ​(ℋ−V)​V1I-iV_{2}e^{i\tau({\mathcal{H}}-V)}V_{1} in Lτ2​H˙yσL^{2}_{\tau}\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{y}, it further boils down to the invertibility of its τ\tau-Fourier transform I+V2​(ℋ−V−z)−1​V1I+V_{2}({\mathcal{H}}-V-z)^{-1}V_{1} in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} and some compactness. Hence the uniform invertibility of (ℋ−z)−1​Pess({\mathcal{H}}-z)^{-1}P_{\rm ess} implies a Strichartz estimate for the modified system

i​∂tZ+ℋ​Pess+i​μ​Pdisc=F\displaystyle i\partial_{t}Z+{\mathcal{H}}P_{\rm ess}+i\mu P_{\rm disc}=F

which captures the evolution of the original system in Pess​H˙σP_{\rm ess}\dot{H}^{\sigma} and concludes the proof in Section 5.

1.5.2. Proof of H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} stability

In Section 6, we prove Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4. We start by introducing JJ-invariance to connect (NLS) with the spectrally decoupled system. The Strichartz and spectral gap enables us to construct the solution for any given center-stable initial datum through contraction mapping (namely Lyapunov-Perron method, see for example [60]). As a corollary, we have a nonlinear unstable-data map from center-stable initial data to the unstable data leading to blowup (Theorem 6.4). One difficulty comes from the nonlinear estimates in Appendix C, where we take DσD^{\sigma} derivative for a CβC^{\beta} nonlinearity with possibly β<σ\beta<\sigma by exploiting the non-vanishing of QbQ_{b}.

For Theorem 1.4, instead of introducing modulation parameters, track its evolution and redo the construction, we use a Brouwer argument to match initial data, inspired by Donninger-Shörkhuber [15]. Specifically, for general initial data, we find the suitable symmetry transformation to shift it onto the blowup manifold constructed in Theorem 1.1. The mode stability Assumption 1.2 ensures the degree of freedom equals the lack of codimensions and non-degeneracy. This argument not only simplifies the proof by avoiding modulation argument, but also enables more time-independent tools like the Strichartz estimates for stability problem.

1.5.3. Proof of H1H^{1} stability

Finally, we prove the H1H^{1} result Theorem 1.5 in Section 7. In order to generalize from H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} stability theory, we introduce the modified spectral projections for localization and H˙σ∩H˙1\dot{H}^{\sigma}\cap\dot{H}^{1} Strichartz estimate for improving regularity.

Critical decay of self-similar profile is a universal difficulty for obtaining localized blowup solution (for instance in fluid [18], dispersive [49, 32], or parabolic problems [38]). Instead of introducing time-dependent damped profiles, we apply the approach from [38] to reparametrize the spectral decomposition and localize the eigenmodes from discrete spectrum (Lemma 7.1). Interestingly, this argument also helps with the improvement of regularity, since stable eigenmodes have oscillatory nature and may not belong to H˙1\dot{H}^{1}.

The H˙σ∩H˙1\dot{H}^{\sigma}\cap\dot{H}^{1} Strichartz estimate (Lemma 7.2) follows from differentiating the equation and commutator estimates of residuals. Then like Theorem 6.4, we can construct unstable-data map in H˙σ∩H˙1\dot{H}^{\sigma}\cap\dot{H}^{1} with modified spectral projections, which can lead to localized blowup datum. Then the proof of Theorem 1.5 comes as in Section 6 for H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} results.

2.2. Extended resolvent families

Using Laplace transform, we can define the resolvent of Δb\Delta_{b} through the free evolution ei​t​Δbe^{it\Delta_{b}}

Rb+​(z)\displaystyle R_{b}^{+}(z) =\displaystyle= i​∫0∞ei​t​Δb​ei​t​z​𝑑t,ℑ⁡z>0;\displaystyle i\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{it\Delta_{b}}e^{itz}dt,\quad\quad\quad\Im z>0; (2.7)

They satisfy the following resolvent properties:

Lemma 2.3 (Resolvent properties).

Let b≠0b\neq 0. For ℑ⁡z>0\Im z>0, the resolvent Rb+​(z)R^{+}_{b}(z) satisfies (similarly for Rb−​(z)R^{-}_{b}(z) with ℑ⁡z<0\Im z<0):

Proof.

This is classical operator semigroup theory [19, Chap.2 Thm. 1.10]. ∎

However, the self-similar dispersive estimate (2.5) indicates the integral in (2.7) to converge in ℒ⁡(Lp′→Lp){\mathcal{L}}(L^{p^{\prime}}\to L^{p}) for some 2<p<2∗2<p<2^{*} as ℑ⁡z>−|b|​min⁡{d2,1}\Im z>-|b|\min\{\frac{d}{2},1\}. Thus we call them extended resolvent family in a larger range of zz. The rest of this subsection is devoted to showing these extended resolvent families retain resolvent properties as Lemma 2.3 in a modified sense.

2.2.3. Resolvent identity and differentiability

Although resolvent identities formally hold, it is not trivial to see how extended resolvents compose with ℒ⁡(Lp′→Lp)\mathcal{L}(L^{p^{\prime}}\to L^{p}) no longer an algebra. The following lemma rigorously verifies such resolvent identities. In particular, the composition makes sense as an operator from Lp′L^{p^{\prime}} to LpL^{p}.

5. Abstract Wiener’s Theorem and Proof of Strichartz estimates

In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.6. We first recall the abstract Wiener’s theorem of Beceanu from [4] (also [3]), and then present the proof of our Strichartz estimates by verifying conditions for a modified Schrödinger system.

5.1. Abstract Wiener’s Theorem

In this subsection, we introduce the setting and abstract tool in Beceanu’s work [4, 3], and then present a version for our later use.

Let HH be a complex Hilbert space, ℒ⁡(H)\mathcal{L}(H) be the space of bounded linear operators from HH to itself, and Lt1​ℒ​(H)L^{1}_{t}\mathcal{L}(H) be the Banach space of operator-valued L1L^{1} functions on ℝ\mathbb{R}. We add a convolutional unit

IK:=δt=0​IHI_{K}:=\delta_{t=0}I_{H}

to define the normed vector space KK

K\displaystyle K :⁣=\displaystyle:= Lt1​ℒ​(H)⊕ℂ⁡{IK};\displaystyle L^{1}_{t}\mathcal{L}(H)\oplus\mathbb{C}\{I_{K}\}; (5.1)
‖μ+a​IK‖K\displaystyle\|\mu+aI_{K}\|_{K} :⁣=\displaystyle:= ‖μ‖Lt1​ℒ​(H)+|a|,∀a∈ℂ,μ∈Lt1​ℒ​(H).\displaystyle\|\mu\|_{L^{1}_{t}\mathcal{L}(H)}+|a|,\qquad\forall a\in\mathbb{C},\,\,\mu\in L^{1}_{t}\mathcal{L}(H). (5.2)

Then it satisfies the following properties:

Lemma 5.1 (Properties of KK).

Let KK defined as (5.1). Then the following statements are true.

  1. (1)

    KK is an unital Banach algebra.

  2. (2)

    Multiplication by bounded continuous functions is bounded on KK:

    ‖f​k‖K≤‖f‖C0​(ℝ)​‖k‖K.\|fk\|_{K}\leq\|f\|_{C^{0}(\mathbb{R})}\|k\|_{K}. (5.3)
  3. (3)

    If k=μ⁡(t)+a​IK∈Kk=\mu(t)+aI_{K}\in K, then k∗=μ​(t)∗+a¯​IK∈Kk^{*}=\mu(t)^{*}+{\overline{a}}I_{K}\in K as well.

  4. (4)

    The Fourier transform is well-defined by

    k^​(λ):=∫ℝe−i​t​λ​k​(t)​𝑑t,\hat{k}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-it\lambda}k(t)dt, (5.4)

    which satisfies ‖k^‖Cλ0​ℒ​(H)≤‖k‖K\|\hat{k}\|_{C^{0}_{\lambda}\mathcal{L}(H)}\leq\|k\|_{K}.

Proof.

The algebra structure is given by Lt1L^{1}_{t}-convolution

(μ+a​IK)∗(ν+b​IK)=μ∗ν+a​ν+b​μ+a​b​IK.(\mu+aI_{K})*(\nu+bI_{K})=\mu*\nu+a\nu+b\mu+abI_{K}.

Then all these properties are trivial. ∎

We stress that the invertibility of k∈Kk\in K means there exists k−1∈Kk^{-1}\in K such that k∗k−1=k−1∗k=IKk*k^{-1}=k^{-1}*k=I_{K}.

Now we are in place to state the abstract Wiener’s theorem, a sufficient condition for k∈Kk\in K to be invertible characterized by invertibility of k^​(λ)∈ℒ​(H)\hat{k}(\lambda)\in\mathcal{L}(H) for all λ\lambda. We also collect the criterion for the upper triangular property (meaning that A∈KA\in K is supported on [0,∞)[0,\infty)) to be preserved under inversion.

Theorem 5.2 ([3, Theorem 3.3], [4, Theorem 2.3], ).

Let KK be the operator algebra of (5.1). If A∈KA\in K is invertible, then A^​(λ)∈ℒ​(H)\hat{A}(\lambda)\in\mathcal{L}(H) is invertible for every λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. Conversely, assume A^​(λ)\hat{A}(\lambda) is invertible for each λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, A−IK=L∈Lt1​(ℒ⁡(H))A-I_{K}=L\in L^{1}_{t}(\mathcal{L}(H)), and

limε→0∥L(⋅+ε)−L∥K=0,limR→∞∥1−ψ(t/R)L(t)∥K=0\mathop{\rm lim}_{\varepsilon\to 0}\|L(\cdot+\varepsilon)-L\|_{K}=0,\quad\mathop{\rm lim}_{R\to\infty}\|1-\psi(t/R)L(t)\|_{K}=0 (5.5)

where ψ∈Cc∞​([−2,2])\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c}([-2,2]) satisfies ψ⁡(t)=1\psi(t)=1 for t∈[−1,1]t\in[-1,1]. Then AA is invertible and A−1−IK∈Lt1​(ℒ⁡(H))A^{-1}-I_{K}\in L^{1}_{t}(\mathcal{L}(H)).

Lemma 5.3 ([3, Lemma 3.4], [4, Lemma 2.5]).

Given A∈KA\in K upper triangular with A−1∈KA^{-1}\in K, A−1A^{-1} is upper triangular if and only if A^\hat{A} can be extended to a weakly analytic family of invertible operators in the lower half-plane (namely it is continuous up to the boundary, uniformly bounded, and has uniformly bounded inverse).

Lemma 5.4.

from Young’s inequality. And similar for ∫0tA−1​(t−s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}A^{-1}(t-s)ds. That ∫0tA−1​(t−s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}A^{-1}(t-s)ds is the inverse of ∫0tA⁡(t−s)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t}A(t-s)ds can be checked using A−1∗A=A∗A−1=IKA^{-1}*A=A*A^{-1}=I_{K}. ∎

Appendix A Fractional Non-stationary Phase

In Lemma 2.9 and Lemma 2.10, we want to make use of the HδH^{\delta}-regularity to integrate by parts and get decay from the quadratic oscillatory phase. For δ<1\delta<1, we achieve this via mollification, with the mollifier’s size adapted to the decay r−1r^{-1} we gain. The idea of this part is credited to Xiaodong Li.

Lemma A.1.

Let smooth cutoff function ψ∈Cc,r​a​d∞​(ℝd)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c,rad}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), supp​ψ⊂B2{\rm supp}~\psi\subset B_{2}, non-negative and ∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)dx=1. Define the rescaling of ψ\psi (or general Cc∞C^{\infty}_{c} functions) by ψλ​(r):=λ−d​ψ​(λ−1​r)\psi_{\lambda}(r):=\lambda^{-d}\psi(\lambda^{-1}r). For f∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)f\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), we have

‖f∗ψ|⋅|−1‖L2{|x|≥1/2}\displaystyle\left\|f*\psi_{|\cdot|^{-1}}\right\|_{L^{2}\{|x|\geq 1/2\}} ≲ψ,d\displaystyle\lesssim_{\psi,d} ‖f‖L2\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{2}} (A.1)
‖∂r(f∗ψ|⋅|−1)|⋅|−1+δ‖L2{|x|≥1/2}\displaystyle\left\|\partial_{r}(f*\psi_{|\cdot|^{-1}})|\cdot|^{-1+\delta}\right\|_{L^{2}\{|x|\geq 1/2\}} ≲ψ,d,δ\displaystyle\lesssim_{\psi,d,\delta} ‖f‖Hδ\displaystyle\|f\|_{H^{\delta}} (A.2)
‖(f−f∗ψ|⋅|−1)|⋅|δ‖L2{|x|≥1/2}\displaystyle\left\|\left(f-f*\psi_{|\cdot|^{-1}}\right)|\cdot|^{\delta}\right\|_{L^{2}\{|x|\geq 1/2\}} ≲ψ,d,δ\displaystyle\lesssim_{\psi,d,\delta} ‖f‖Hδ\displaystyle\|f\|_{H^{\delta}} (A.3)

where (A.1) also holds for general ψ∈Cc∞​(B2)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(B_{2}) with constant depending on ψ\psi.

Proof.

Appendix B Commutator estimates of multiplication in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma}

We consider several boundedness and commutator estimates for scalar potential VV in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma}. Recall our polynomial decay assumption on potential

|V⁡(x)|≲⟨x⟩−α,|∇V​(x)|≲⟨x⟩−α−1|V(x)|\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha},\quad|\nabla V(x)|\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha-1} (1.27)

for some α>0\alpha>0.

Lemma B.1.

For d≥1d\geq 1, 0<σ<min⁡{1,d2}0<\sigma<\min\left\{1,\frac{d}{2}\right\} and V∈C1​(ℝd)V\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), for 2≤p<dσ2\leq p<\frac{d}{\sigma},

∥DσVD−σ∥L2→Lp′+∥DσVD−σ∥Lp→L2≲d,p,σ∥V∥W˙σ,(12+σd−1p)−1\|D^{\sigma}VD^{-\sigma}\|_{L^{2}\to L^{p^{\prime}}}+\|D^{\sigma}VD^{-\sigma}\|_{L^{p}\to L^{2}}\lesssim_{d,p,\sigma}\|V\|_{\dot{W}^{\sigma,\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sigma}{d}-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{-1}}} (B.1)

In particular, for VV satisfying (1.27) with α>0\alpha>0, Dσ​V​D−σ∈ℒ⁡(L2→Lp′)∩ℒ⁡(Lp→L2)D^{\sigma}VD^{-\sigma}\in\mathcal{L}(L^{2}\to L^{p^{\prime}})\cap\mathcal{L}(L^{p}\to L^{2}) for 12≥1p>max⁡{12−αd,σd}\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{1}{p}>\max\{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{d},\frac{\sigma}{d}\}.

Proof.

It is an easy application of Sobolev embedding and the fractional Lebnitz rule (see for example [27, Theorem 1])

∥Ds(f1f2)∥Lr≲d,s,r,p1,p2,q1,q2∥Dsf1∥Lp1∥f2∥Lq1+∥f1∥Lp2∥Dsf2∥Lq2\|D^{s}(f_{1}f_{2})\|_{L^{r}}\lesssim_{d,s,r,p_{1},p_{2},q_{1},q_{2}}\|D^{s}f_{1}\|_{L^{p_{1}}}\|f_{2}\|_{L^{q_{1}}}+\|f_{1}\|_{L^{p_{2}}}\|D^{s}f_{2}\|_{L^{q_{2}}} (B.2)

with 1>s>01>s>0, r∈(1,∞)r\in(1,\infty), p1,p2,q1,q2∈(1,∞]p_{1},p_{2},q_{1},q_{2}\in(1,\infty] satisfying 1r=1p1+1q1=1p2+1q2\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{p_{1}}+\frac{1}{q_{1}}=\frac{1}{p_{2}}+\frac{1}{q_{2}} and f,g∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)f,g\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). ∎

Moreover, the shape of VV indicates a stronger bound: ‖⟨x⟩α​V​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2\|\langle x\rangle^{\alpha}Vf\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}} in L2L^{2}. This remains almost true after conjugating VV with fractional derivatives.

Lemma B.2.

Let d≥1d\geq 1, 0<σ<min⁡{1,d2}0<\sigma<\min\left\{1,\frac{d}{2}\right\} and V∈C1​(ℝd)V\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfying (1.27) with parameter α>0\alpha>0. We have the following statements:

  1. (i)

    For 0≤β<min⁡{α,1}0\leq\beta<\min\left\{\alpha,1\right\} and any f∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)f\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we have

    ‖⟨x⟩β​Dσ​V​D−σ​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2.\|\langle x\rangle^{\beta}D^{\sigma}VD^{-\sigma}f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}. (B.3)
  2. (ii)

    For 0≤β<min⁡{α,d2−σ}0\leq\beta<\min\{\alpha,\frac{d}{2}-\sigma\} and f∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)f\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we have

    ‖⟨x⟩β​D−σ​V​Dσ​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2\|\langle x\rangle^{\beta}D^{-\sigma}VD^{\sigma}f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}} (B.4)
  3. (iii)

    Let 0<α+β<γ<10<\alpha+\beta<\gamma<1, we have

    ‖⟨x⟩α​Dσ​⟨⋅⟩β​D−σ​⟨⋅⟩−γ​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2.\|\langle x\rangle^{\alpha}D^{\sigma}\langle\cdot\rangle^{\beta}D^{-\sigma}\langle\cdot\rangle^{-\gamma}f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}. (B.5)

    Consequently, ⟨x⟩β∈ℒ⁡(H˙⟨x⟩γσ→H˙⟨x⟩ασ)\langle x\rangle^{\beta}\in\mathcal{L}(\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{\langle x\rangle^{\gamma}}\to\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{\langle x\rangle^{\alpha}}).

  4. (iv)

    Suppose additionally V∈C2​(ℝd)V\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and |∇2V​(x)|≲⟨x⟩−α−2|\nabla^{2}V(x)|\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha-2}, then for r<dσr<\frac{d}{\sigma}, 1q+1r∈(1−σd,1)\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{r}\in(1-\frac{\sigma}{d},1), we have

    ‖Dσ​[V,D1−σ]​D−σ​f‖Lr′≲‖f‖Lq.\|D^{\sigma}[V,D^{1-\sigma}]D^{-\sigma}f\|_{L^{r^{\prime}}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{q}}. (B.6)

    Consequently, [V,D1−σ]∈ℒ⁡(W˙σ,q→W˙σ,r′)[V,D^{1-\sigma}]\in{\mathcal{L}}(\dot{W}^{\sigma,q}\to\dot{W}^{\sigma,r^{\prime}}).

Proof.

(i) Since ⟨x⟩β​V\langle x\rangle^{\beta}V satisfies the polynomial decay condition (1.27) with parameter α−β>0\alpha-\beta>0, Lemma B.1 suggests that it suffices to estimate the commutator

‖[Dσ,⟨⋅⟩β]​V​D−σ​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2.\left\|[D^{\sigma},\langle\cdot\rangle^{\beta}]VD^{-\sigma}f\right\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}. (B.7)

Without less of generality, we assume α∈(β,1)\alpha\in(\beta,1).

With the physical representation of DσD^{\sigma} and the cancellation from the commutator, we have the decomposition

|[Dσ,⟨⋅⟩β]​V​D−σ​f|​(x)=C​|∫ℝd⟨x⟩β−⟨x−y⟩β|y|d+σ​(V​D−σ​f)​(x−y)​𝑑y|\displaystyle\left|[D^{\sigma},\langle\cdot\rangle^{\beta}]VD^{-\sigma}f\right|(x)=C\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\langle x\rangle^{\beta}-\langle x-y\rangle^{\beta}}{|y|^{d+\sigma}}(VD^{-\sigma}f)(x-y)dy\right|
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∫|y|≥2​⟨x⟩|y|−(d+σ+α−β)(|⋅|−(d−σ)∗|f|)(x−y)dy\displaystyle\int_{|y|\geq 2\langle x\rangle}|y|^{-(d+\sigma+\alpha-\beta)}\left(|\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}*|f|\right)(x-y)dy (B.8)
+\displaystyle+ ∫|y|≤2​⟨x⟩|y|−(d+σ−1)⟨x⟩β−1⟨x−y⟩−α[(|⋅|−(d−σ)𝟙B4​⟨x⟩)∗|f|](x−y)dy\displaystyle\int_{|y|\leq 2\langle x\rangle}|y|^{-(d+\sigma-1)}\langle x\rangle^{\beta-1}\langle x-y\rangle^{-\alpha}\left[\left(|\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{4\langle x\rangle}}\right)*|f|\right](x-y)dy (B.9)
+\displaystyle+ ∫|y|≤2​⟨x⟩|y|−(d+σ−1)⟨x⟩β−1⟨x−y⟩−α[(|⋅|−(d−σ)𝟙B4​⟨x⟩c)∗|f|](x−y)dy\displaystyle\int_{|y|\leq 2\langle x\rangle}|y|^{-(d+\sigma-1)}\langle x\rangle^{\beta-1}\langle x-y\rangle^{-\alpha}\left[\left(|\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{4\langle x\rangle}^{c}}\right)*|f|\right](x-y)dy (B.10)

where |V||V| is substituted by ⟨x⟩−α\langle x\rangle^{-\alpha} and the fractional weight is bounded by

|⟨x⟩β−⟨x−y⟩β|​⟨x−y⟩−α≲{|y|β−α|y|≥2​⟨x⟩,|y|​⟨x⟩β−1​⟨x−y⟩−α|y|≤2​⟨x⟩.\left|\langle x\rangle^{\beta}-\langle x-y\rangle^{\beta}\right|\langle x-y\rangle^{-\alpha}\lesssim\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}|y|^{\beta-\alpha}&|y|\geq 2\langle x\rangle,\\ |y|\langle x\rangle^{\beta-1}\langle x-y\rangle^{-\alpha}&|y|\leq 2\langle x\rangle.\end{array}\right.

Now we will bound the L2L^{2}-norm of (B.8)-(B.10) with ‖f‖L2\|f\|_{L^{2}}.

For (B.8), using Hölder and Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality, we get

(B.8)≲∥|⋅|−(d+σ+α−β)∥L2​dd+2​σ​(B2​⟨x⟩c)∥|⋅|−(d−σ)∗f∥L2​dd−2​σ≲⟨x⟩−d2−α+β∥f∥L2.\displaystyle\eqref{eqcom01}\lesssim\||\cdot|^{-(d+\sigma+\alpha-\beta)}\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d+2\sigma}}(B_{2\langle x\rangle}^{c})}\||\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}*f\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d-2\sigma}}}\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\frac{d}{2}-\alpha+\beta}\|f\|_{L^{2}}.

Since α>β\alpha>\beta, we get ‖(B.8)‖L2≲‖f‖L2\|\eqref{eqcom01}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}.

For (B.9), noticing that |z|≥4​⟨x⟩|z|\geq 4\langle x\rangle and |y|≤2​⟨x⟩|y|\leq 2\langle x\rangle imply |x−y−z|∼|z||x-y-z|\sim|z|, so

(B.9)≲⟨x⟩β−1​∫B2​⟨x⟩|y|−(d+σ−1)​⟨x−y⟩−α​𝑑y​∫B4​⟨x⟩c|f⁡(z)||z|d−σ​𝑑z≲⟨x⟩−d2−α+β​‖f‖L2\displaystyle\eqref{eqcom02}\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{\beta-1}\int_{B_{2\langle x\rangle}}|y|^{-(d+\sigma-1)}\langle x-y\rangle^{-\alpha}dy\int_{B_{4\langle x\rangle}^{c}}\frac{|f(z)|}{|z|^{d-\sigma}}dz\lesssim\langle x\rangle^{-\frac{d}{2}-\alpha+\beta}\|f\|_{L^{2}}

where the first integral is bounded by ⟨x⟩1−σ−α\langle x\rangle^{1-\sigma-\alpha} when α<d\alpha<d via elementary computation. Therefore this term has the desired bound.

Finally, we write (B.10) as

(B.10)=⟨x⟩β−1(|⋅|−(d+σ−1)𝟙B2​⟨x⟩)∗[⟨⋅⟩−α𝟙B3​⟨x⟩(|⋅|−(d−σ)𝟙B4​⟨x⟩∗|f|)](x).\displaystyle\eqref{eqcom03}=\langle x\rangle^{\beta-1}\left(|\cdot|^{-(d+\sigma-1)}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{2\langle x\rangle}}\right)*\left[\langle\cdot\rangle^{-\alpha}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{3\langle x\rangle}}\left(|\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{4\langle x\rangle}}*|f|\right)\right](x).

Then we can estimate their L2L^{2} norm on dyadic annulus with k≥0k\geq 0

‖(B.10)‖L2​(B2k+1−B2k)\displaystyle\|\eqref{eqcom03}\|_{L^{2}(B_{2^{k+1}}-B_{2^{k}})} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−k⁡(1−β)∥|⋅|−(d+σ−1)∥Lp1​(B2k+3)∥⟨⋅⟩−α∥Lp2​(B2k+3)\displaystyle 2^{-k(1-\beta)}\||\cdot|^{-(d+\sigma-1)}\|_{L^{p_{1}}(B_{2^{k+3}})}\|\langle\cdot\rangle^{-\alpha}\|_{L^{p_{2}}(B_{2^{k+3}})}
⋅∥|⋅|−(d−σ)∥Lp3​(B2k+3)∥f∥L2\displaystyle\cdot\||\cdot|^{-(d-\sigma)}\|_{L^{p_{3}}(B_{2^{k+3}})}\|f\|_{L^{2}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−k⁡(α−β)​‖f‖L2.\displaystyle 2^{-k(\alpha-\beta)}\|f\|_{L^{2}}.

where we choose p1,p2,p3∈(1,∞)p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}\in(1,\infty) such that 1p1+1p2+1p3=2\frac{1}{p_{1}}+\frac{1}{p_{2}}+\frac{1}{p_{3}}=2, p1<dd+σ−1p_{1}<\frac{d}{d+\sigma-1}, p2<dαp_{2}<\frac{d}{\alpha} and p3<dd−σp_{3}<\frac{d}{d-\sigma} which is possible when α<1\alpha<1. The contribution on B1B_{1} can be bounded similarly, and we conclude the estimate of (B.10) by summing all these estimates up using α>β\alpha>\beta.

Combining these three parts, we obtain (B.7) and hence (B.3).

(ii) Without loss of generality, we assume α<d2−σ\alpha<\frac{d}{2}-\sigma. Because ⟨x⟩β​V∈L∞\langle x\rangle^{\beta}V\in L^{\infty}, it suffices to show

‖⟨x⟩β​D−σ​[Dσ,V]​f‖L2≲‖f‖L2.\left\|\langle x\rangle^{\beta}D^{-\sigma}[D^{\sigma},V]f\right\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}. (B.11)

Notice that

⟨x⟩β​D−σ​[Dσ,V]​f​(x)\displaystyle\langle x\rangle^{\beta}D^{-\sigma}[D^{\sigma},V]f(x)
=\displaystyle= C​⟨x⟩β​∫ℝd1|y|d−σ​∫ℝdV⁡(x−y)−V⁡(x−y−z)|z|d+σ​f​(x−y−z)​𝑑z​𝑑y.\displaystyle C\langle x\rangle^{\beta}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{|y|^{d-\sigma}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{V(x-y)-V(x-y-z)}{|z|^{d+\sigma}}f(x-y-z)dzdy.

When pp is large, these estimates easily follow the fractional chain rule for F′′​(W+t​ε)F^{\prime\prime}(W+t\varepsilon) with F⁡(z):=|z|p−1​zF(z):=|z|^{p-1}z. ‖F‖W˙σ,r1′\displaystyle\|F\|_{\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}^{\prime}}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖Z‖W˙σ,r1∩W˙σ,r1−p,‖V​Z‖W˙σ,r1′≲‖Z‖W˙σ,r1.\displaystyle\|Z\|_{\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}}\cap\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}^{-}}}^{p},\quad\|VZ\|_{\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}^{\prime}}}\lesssim\|Z\|_{\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}}}.

Like (6.2), the space-time estimate follows

‖F−V​Z‖Lτq1′​W˙yσ,r1′≲(‖Z‖Y~dp+‖Z‖Y~d)​Tβ\displaystyle\|F-VZ\|_{L^{q_{1}^{\prime}}_{\tau}\dot{W}^{\sigma,r_{1}^{\prime}}_{y}}\lesssim(\|Z\|_{\tilde{Y}_{d}}^{p}+\|Z\|_{\tilde{Y}_{d}})T^{\beta}

Now the Strichartz estimate for ei​t​(ℋb−i​b​sc)e^{it({\mathcal{H}}_{b}-ibs_{c})} in H˙σ\dot{H}^{\sigma} yields the onto estimate straightforwardly.

As for the contraction estimate, notice that

|R⁡(Z1,Qb)−R⁡(Z1′,Qb)|≲|Z1−Z1′|(|Z1|p−1+|Z1′|p−1+|Qb|p−1).\displaystyle|R(Z_{1},Q_{b})-R(Z_{1}^{\prime},Q_{b})|\lesssim|Z_{1}-Z_{1}^{\prime}|(|Z_{1}|^{p-1}+|Z_{1}^{\prime}|^{p-1}+|Q_{b}|^{p-1}).

Then mimicking Proposition D.1, we get

‖(F−V​Z)−(F′−V​Z′)‖Lτq0′​Lyr0′≲‖Z−Z′‖Lτq0​Lyr0​(‖Z‖Lτ∞​H˙yσp−1+‖Z′‖Lτ∞​H˙yσp−1+‖Qb‖H˙σp−1)​Tβ\displaystyle\|(F-VZ)-(F^{\prime}-VZ^{\prime})\|_{L^{q_{0}^{\prime}}_{\tau}L^{r_{0}^{\prime}}_{y}}\lesssim\|Z-Z^{\prime}\|_{L^{q_{0}}_{\tau}L^{r_{0}}_{y}}\left(\|Z\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{y}}^{p-1}+\|Z^{\prime}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{y}}^{p-1}+\|Q_{b}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}^{p-1}\right)T^{\beta}

which suffices to conclude the contraction estimate.

∎
